title: UN warns Sri Lanka risks failing FATF test with blanket curbs | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 18 September 2026 00:00
-     - 8

Resident Coordinator in Sri Lanka Marc-André Franche 

        - Pic by Daminda Harsha Perera

UN Resident Coordinator in Sri Lanka Marc-André Franche yesterday said Sri Lanka risks undermining the same security and development goals its anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing (AML/CFT) rules are meant to serve if those rules are applied as blanket restrictions on civil society rather than through targeted risk assessment.

His remarks came as Sri Lanka undergoes it third Mutual Evaluation process on AML/CFT with the Asia-Pacific Group on Money Laundering (APG), the regional body affiliated with the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). 

Speaking at the launch of the Sri Lanka Civil Society FATF Shadow Report, organised by the Sri Lanka CSO FATF Network, Franche said the FATF’s Recommendation 8 exists because terrorist organisations have exploited non-profits’ public trust and relatively light oversight to move and disguise money. 

He said the standard’s original 2001 approach led many countries into broad, one-size-fits-all restrictions on the entire non-profit sector, straining legitimate charitable work without meaningfully reducing risk. 

A 2023 revision to the standard narrowed its focus to organisations actually facing high risk, and required governments to assess that risk individually rather than regulate all non-profits uniformly, he said.

“If it’s applied well, in a targeted, focused, proportionate, and evidence-based way, as it is intended, it strengthens security, civic space, and it will enable development and growth of this country,” Franche said. “If it is applied as a blanket measure, it will do the opposite.”

The report launched at the event found that Sri Lanka’s regulatory measures, introduced under the justification of meeting FATF requirements ahead of the Mutual Evaluation, have instead constrained non-profit organisations broadly. 

A 2025 survey of 102 non-profits found 69% had experienced difficulties receiving foreign funds, with at least 42% of those told by banks to register with the Non-Governmental Organisations (NGO) Secretariat to receive such funds, a requirement not stipulated by law. Nearly half of respondents reported difficulty opening new bank accounts, and only 17% reported no issues at all.

Franche said Sri Lanka has “a documented tendency to broadly interpret or over-apply security measures,” pointing to how the Prevention of Terrorism Act has been used against civil society, journalists, and minority groups. 

He said 2026 amendments to the Financial Transaction Reporting Act, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, and the Convention on Suppression of Terrorist Financing Act have expanded investigative, surveillance, and asset-management powers, while a proposed law on NGO registration and supervision raises further concerns the UN has already conveyed to the Government about replicating powers associated with the Prevention of Terrorism Act.

He said UN human rights treaty bodies have separately raised concerns about funding restrictions and bureaucratic obstacles facing non-governmental organisations, including registration and clearance requirements that contradict human rights law.

Franche called for an enabling regulatory environment built on institutionalised, inclusive consultation, with draft legislation published with adequate time for review in local languages, arguing this was absent from the current legislative process. 

He said laws governing civil society should provide safeguards against arbitrary detention, disproportionate surveillance, and unjustified asset seizure without due process, while ensuring continued access to banking and protection for humanitarian and disaster-response activity.

Protecting civic space was not a concession to civil society but an investment in the country’s resilience, Franche said, noting the sector’s role in the humanitarian response to Cyclone Ditwah in November 2025, which affected an estimated 2.2 million people. 

He said no major challenge facing Sri Lanka, including poverty reduction, could be resolved by Government alone without a functioning civil society and private sector alongside it.

The UN, he said, stood ready to support an approach to the Mutual Evaluation that is evidence-based and proportionate.

title: Energy Committee endorses petroleum exploration licensing round | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 18 September 2026 00:21
-     - 5

The Ministerial Consultative Committee on Energy Affairs has approved the order governing the calling of investment proposals for the exploration and development of petroleum resources in Sri Lanka, opening the exploration round to the world on 25 August.

The approval was granted at a meeting of the Committee held at Parliament recently, chaired by Energy Minister Anura Karunathilaka.

The order was issued by the Energy Minister under Section 48 of the Petroleum Resources Act, No. 21 of 2021, read with Section 17 of the Act, and had been approved by the Cabinet of Ministers as part of its issuance. It was published in Extraordinary Gazette No. 2497/37 dated 16 July 2026.

Under the order, any party seeking to explore or develop petroleum resources in one or more identified blocks must submit an investment proposal, along with the administrative fee specified in the relevant invitation for bids.

The round, designated Sri Lanka Licensing Round 2026 (SL2026-01), offers four offshore exploration blocks spanning nearly 34,000 square kilometres in the Mannar Basin. 

Petroleum Development Authority of Sri Lanka (PDASL) Director General Dr. Neil De Silva said bids were expected to close in early 2027, followed by evaluation and the award of blocks through Petroleum Resources Agreements, with commercial production targeted by 2032 if commercially viable resources are established.

An international investor campaign is running alongside the bidding process. Engagement begins in London at the World Energies Summit on 29 and 30 September, followed by a virtual investor briefing on 21 October and investor engagement in Kuala Lumpur at the Asia Petroleum Geoscience Conference and Exhibition on 16 and 17 November.

Sri Lanka already has two gas discoveries in the Mannar Basin, Dorado, and Barracuda, both made in 2011, with a combined P50 resource estimate of 839 billion cubic feet. P50 denotes the most-likely estimate, meaning there is a 50% probability the actual resource will equal or exceed that volume.

title: US Fed hikes interest rates for first time in three years | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 18 September 2026 00:20
-     - 6

i

The US Federal Reserve has raised interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% as inflation, driven by soaring fuel prices amid the US-Iran war, continues to weigh on the economy.

It is the first hike in more than three years and comes just weeks before the US midterm elections, despite repeated demands from US President Donald Trump to lower rates.

“Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient,” the Fed said in a statement on Wednesday. “Inflation remains elevated. Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2% goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.”

Nearly three hours after the interest rate decision, Trump posted on Truth Social, his social media platform, that “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — by far. Our country is booming with new Investment!” He added, “Lower the interest rates for the United States of America, and fast!”
